Lately I have been thinking about the unfinished. Not as failure, but as a kind of mercy.

There is a strange pressure in the world to complete things: to finish the book, to answer the last email, to resolve the argument, to become a finished version of oneself. But I have started to suspect that the unfinished has its own quiet wisdom. An unfinished sentence can hold more truth than a polished paragraph. A half-read novel can linger in the mind for years, not because of what it said, but because of what it never got the chance to say.

Consider the unfinished symphony, the abandoned painting, the letter written but never sent. These things are often more alive than their completed counterparts because they still contain every possible ending. The moment a thing is finished, it becomes fixed. It is no longer becoming. But an unfinished thing remains open—a door ajar, a question still breathing.

I think of Gaudí’s Sagrada Família, still under construction after more than a century. People travel from all over the world to see a building that is not done. Maybe that is exactly why they go. It is a cathedral that still believes in its own future. It has not hardened into a monument. It is still on its way.

The same is true of people. We are all unfinished. We speak of self-improvement as if one day we will arrive, complete and gleaming, at the final version of ourselves. But no one ever does. We are always mid-sentence, mid-thought, mid-becoming. And that is not a deficiency. It is the condition of being alive.

Even our conversations are full of unfinished things. A friend says, “I don’t know, I just feel like—” and then trails off. And somehow the trailing off says more than the words could have. The silence completes the thought in a way language could not. We understand each other not only through what is said, but through what is left hanging in the air.

There is also a kind of grief in the unfinished. The relationship that ended without closure. The project abandoned in a drawer. The goodbye that never happened. But maybe closure is overrated. Maybe some doors are meant to stay open. Maybe the unfinished is not a wound that needs healing, but a space that needs tending—a place where something new can still enter.

So I have been trying to make peace with my own unfinishedness. To stop apologizing for the half-done, the in-progress, the not-yet. To see my life not as a task to be completed, but as a story still being written. The best stories, after all, are the ones that leave a little room for the reader. They do not end so much as they open outward.

Perhaps the most honest thing any of us can say is: *I am not finished.* Not as an excuse, but as a reminder. There is still time. There is still change. There is still the possibility of becoming something we have not yet imagined.

And that, I think, is beautiful.
